title: Evaluating agent performance
notes: A test set is real customer questions with expected outcomes, run the same way every time so scores can be compared.
Check every answer for the right tool, the key facts, policy kept and nothing invented, and track the pass rate after every change.
Read the failures, not just the number: good enough to ship means the failures left are safe.

slides.title: Evaluating agent performance
slides.sub: A test set, four checks and a pass rate you track after every change
sentences: Debugging fixes one case at a time.
Evaluation tells you how Scout does across all of them, and whether a change really helped.
By the end, you'll have a real answer to Maya's favourite question: is it ready?

slides.title: Seems fine versus measured

left.label: Trying it by hand
points: A few questions you thought of
No idea if a change helped

right.label: A test set
points: The same checks on every run

sentences: Most people test an agent by chatting with it.
You try a few questions you thought of, and the answers look fine.
But you can't tell whether yesterday's change helped or hurt.
And things break quietly, in questions you didn't think to ask.
A test set fixes that: real questions, taken from Leo's ticket queue.
Scout answers every one, the same checks run every time, and you get a score you can compare.

slides.title: One test case
slides.lead: Each case is a real question plus what a good answer must, and must not, contain.

rows.out: a real question from a ticket
a fact the reply must contain

aside.label: Where cases come from
aside.text: Leo's queue: the common questions, the awkward ones and the risky ones.

sentences: Here is one test case.
The question is real: Ravi asks whether his order has shipped.
The case says which tool Scout must call: get order.
It lists a fact the reply must contain: his order is still processing.
And it lists something the reply must never contain: a tracking number, because Ravi doesn't have one yet.
Good cases come from real tickets: the common ones, the awkward ones and the risky ones.

slides.title: Four checks on every answer

note.text: A case passes only if all four checks pass.

sentences: Every answer goes through four checks.
Right tool: did Scout call the tool the case expects?
Key facts: does the reply contain what it must, like the arrival day?
Policy kept: no refund approved without a person, and no return outside thirty days.
Nothing invented: no status, date or tracking number that didn't come from a tool.
A case passes only when all four checks pass.

slides.title: From test set to pass rate

note.text: One command runs it all. Run it after every change, and write the score down.

sentences: Put together, an evaluation is a simple pipeline.
The test set feeds in sixty cases.
Scout answers each one, starting from a fresh memory every time.
The checker applies the four checks to every answer.
Out comes a pass rate: here, 53 of 60, or 88 percent.
It's one command, so run it after every change and write the score down.

slides.title: Track it after every change

note.text: A drop is useful: it tells you exactly which change hurt.

sentences: Here is Scout's score history, one line per change.
The first full run scored 38, and 15 of the failures shared one cause.
Letting get order take an email lifted it to 53, and no case that passed before broke.
Then a shorter system prompt dropped it to 50, breaking three return cases, so Priya undid it.
A clearer rule about refund replies took it to 58.
Without the history, that drop to 50 would have slipped through to customers.
Scores can wobble a little between runs, so always look at which cases moved, not just the total.

slides.title: Read the failures, not just the number
sentences: Two agents can both score 90 percent and be very different.
Some failures are unsafe, like approving a big refund without a person, and they block a launch.
Some are wrong, like a made-up arrival date, and they need fixing soon.
Some are just awkward: stiff wording, but the right facts, and they can wait.
So read every failure and sort it, because the number alone can't tell you which kind you have.

slides.title: Good enough to ship
slides.lead: Good enough doesn't mean 100 percent. It means the failures left are safe.

bullets.text: Zero unsafe failures: policy and money rules always kept
Pass rate at or above the target you set when scoping
Every remaining failure read, sorted and understood
People reviewing real chats for the first weeks

aside.label: Maya's question
aside.text: Is it ready? becomes: here is what still fails, and here is why that's safe.

sentences: So when is Scout good enough to ship?
First, zero unsafe failures: the policy and money rules hold in every case.
Second, the pass rate meets the target you set back when you scoped the project.
Third, you have read every remaining failure, and you know why each one is harmless.
Fourth, people review real chats in the first weeks, because no test set covers everything.
Then Maya's question has a real answer: here is what still fails, and here is why that's safe.

slides.title: Recap

points.text: A test set: real questions with expected outcomes.
Four checks: right tool, key facts, policy kept, nothing invented.
Run it after every change and keep the score history.
Ship when the failures left are safe, not when the score is perfect.

sentences: Let's recap.
A test set is real customer questions, each with an expected outcome.
Every answer gets four checks: right tool, key facts, policy kept and nothing invented.
Run it after every change, and keep the history so you can see what helped and what hurt.
And ship when the failures left are safe, not when the score is perfect.
Next, you'll assemble Scout yourself and write its first tests.

midQuiz.q: Why use a fixed test set instead of chatting with Scout to see if a change made it better?
options: It's quicker to type than a chat
The same cases and checks on every run make the scores comparable
Chatting with an agent costs more tokens
midQuiz.explain: A score only means something next to another score from the same cases and checks. That is what tells you whether a change helped or hurt.
midQuiz.hint: What do you need in order to compare two runs?

midQuiz.q: Which of these is a nothing-invented failure?
options: Scout says a parcel arrives Thursday, though track_parcel timed out
Scout says the medium jacket is in stock after check_stock returned 3
Scout asks for an order number when the customer gave none
midQuiz.explain: The arrival day didn't come from any tool: the tracking call failed. Scout made it up, which is exactly what this check catches.
midQuiz.hint: Which fact has no tool result behind it?

endQuiz.q: After a prompt change, Scout's score drops from 53 to 50. What should you do?
options: Read the cases that now fail, to see what the change broke
Ignore it: scores always wobble a little
Delete the cases that now fail
endQuiz.explain: Scores can wobble slightly between runs, so re-run if unsure, but the newly failing cases show exactly where to look. Deleting them only hides the problem.
endQuiz.hint: The total tells you something changed. What tells you what?

endQuiz.q: What does good enough to ship mean in this lesson?
options: Maya has tried it and likes it
The target is met and every failure left is safe
endQuiz.explain: Perfect scores don't exist for real agents. Ship when unsafe failures are at zero, the target is met, every remaining failure is understood, and people watch the first weeks.
endQuiz.hint: It's about what still fails, not about perfection.
